# Isolating Failure in Dual-Fan Radiator Assemblies

Diagnosing a dual-fan radiator assembly on a 2007 Audi A3 2.0 TDI requires understanding how the electrical architecture distributes power and control signals. Based on the wiring you described, you are dealing with a specific topology: two fans connected in series across a single high-current loop (red and brown wires) with separate low-voltage control lines (green and black). This configuration is common in European diesel engines where thermal efficiency demands precise airflow management rather than simple "on/off" operation.

The core challenge here is determining which component has failed without frying your test equipment or damaging the engine's control module. You mentioned using a small 12V battery rated at 27A. Before you connect anything, consider the current draw of these fans. High-performance radiator fans often pull between 30A and 50A combined when running at full speed. Your 27A battery is likely a standard SLA (Sealed Lead Acid) unit or a small jump-start battery, not an engine starter. While it can provide a momentary burst of current, the internal resistance of an SLA battery will cause its voltage to sag significantly under load. When you connect this low-impedance source directly to the fan motor windings, the voltage drop across the battery terminals might prevent the fans from reaching their rated speed, leading to false negatives where a good fan appears sluggish due to poor power delivery rather than internal winding failure.

To safely test the assembly, treat the fan cluster as a black box first. Disconnect the harness from the vehicle's ECU and isolate the physical connectors. You need a dedicated DC power supply capable of delivering at least 50A with adjustable voltage, or a larger lithium jump starter pack designed for automotive use. If you must use your 27A battery, insert an inline fuse rated slightly below your battery's max safe discharge (e.g., 40A) to prevent catastrophic failure if the fan motor shorts internally.

The series connection between the two fans complicates isolation. In a series configuration, the same current flows through both motors. If one fan has an open winding or seized bearings, it creates a high-resistance path that prevents current from reaching the second fan entirely. You cannot test them individually while they remain wired in series. The only way to verify individual health is to physically disconnect the interconnecting wires between the large and small fans. Once separated, you can apply power directly to one motor at a time using a dedicated 12V source.

Observe the behavior of each fan independently. A healthy DC motor should spin up immediately upon voltage application. If a fan hums loudly but does not spin, the bearings are likely seized or the windings have an open circuit. If the fan spins freely but very slowly despite a strong power source, the internal winding resistance is too high, indicating degradation.

The green and black wires represent the control logic. On VW/Audi platforms, the black wire is typically ground, while the green wire carries the PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) signal or a voltage reference from the ECU to modulate fan speed based on coolant temperature. You can test these with a multimeter. Set your meter to measure voltage between the green and black wires while the engine is running and the cooling system is under load. If the voltage fluctuates between 0V and 12V smoothly, the PWM signal is intact. A steady 12V suggests the ECU has commanded maximum speed, while a steady 0V indicates the fan should be off. However, if you have already isolated the fans from the car, these wires will show no voltage unless the ECU is actively communicating via a diagnostic port or you simulate the ground reference.

Do not attempt to test the assembly with your vehicle's battery if the cooling system is hot and the engine block is still pressurized. Thermal expansion can cause leaks at the hose connections near the fans, and an uncontrolled fan spin-up could exacerbate pressure issues. Always allow the engine to cool before removing the radiator shroud or disconnecting high-voltage components.

If your goal extends beyond simple diagnostics to implementing custom cooling control logic in a fleet management system, you might consider integrating these thermal metrics into a broader monitoring stack.
